result: The study analyzed 154 participants with subtype B HIV-1 from the SPARTAC trial, randomized to 48 weeks ART, 12 weeks ART, or no therapy. HIV-1 DNA was measured using validated qPCR assays with coefficient of variance 8.31% for the integration assay.
evaluation: The methodological claims are well-documented with appropriate sample selection criteria (C1, C2), clear trial design (C66-C69), and validated laboratory methods (C70-C72). The coefficient of variance indicates acceptable assay precision, though the integration assay is more complex than the Total DNA assay.

result: At baseline, Total and Integrated HIV-1 DNA levels were closely correlated (r²=0.72, p<0.0001) and both significantly associated with plasma viral load (r²=0.48 and 0.64 respectively) and inversely with CD4 count (r²=0.20 and 0.27), but not with estimated time since seroconversion.
evaluation: The correlations are statistically significant with appropriate sample size (n=154 for Total, n=111 for Integrated). The lack of correlation with time since seroconversion (C10) is interesting but may reflect the narrow window of PHI enrollment. The stronger correlation of Integrated DNA with viral load (r²=0.64 vs 0.48) suggests biological relevance.

result: In untreated patients, lower baseline HIV-1 DNA (both Total and Integrated) predicted delayed clinical progression. In multivariable analysis, Total HIV-1 DNA (HR=3.57, p=0.002) and CD4 count remained significant predictors, while plasma viral load did not (HR=1.25, p=0.33). Integrated DNA did not retain significance in multivariable analysis.
evaluation: The Kaplan-Meier analyses (C11-C16) and Cox regression models (C17-C23) provide converging evidence. The finding that Total DNA outperforms viral load in multivariable models is notable. However, the loss of significance for Integrated DNA in multivariable analysis (C23) contrasts with its univariable significance and warrants further investigation. Sample sizes are adequate (n=51 for Total, n=38 for Integrated).

result: ART reduced HIV-1 DNA levels by 0.63 log copies/million CD4 cells (Total) and 0.59 log (Integrated) after 48 weeks. Total DNA remained significantly higher than Integrated DNA even after 48 weeks of suppressive ART (p=0.027), consistent with persistent unintegrated forms.
evaluation: The decline in HIV-1 DNA on ART is well-documented (C26-C28) with highly significant p-values (p<0.0001). The persistent difference between Total and Integrated DNA (C29) is biologically plausible and supported by prior literature (C30). The interpretation regarding unintegrated forms (C25) is reasonable given established HIV biology.

result: HIV-1 DNA levels at treatment interruption (TI) predicted time to clinical progression. Both Total (HR=3.42, p=0.013) and Integrated (HR=2.81, p=0.04) DNA retained significance in multivariable models with CD4 count, which was not predictive. HIV-1 DNA was the only predictor of the primary endpoint at TI.
evaluation: The survival analyses (C31-C36) and Cox regression models (C37-C43) demonstrate that HIV-1 DNA at TI predicts progression independently of CD4 count. The sample size (n=47) is adequate. The finding that CD4 count is not predictive at TI (C41-C42) when viral load is undetectable highlights the unique value of HIV-1 DNA measurement in this clinical context.

result: HIV-1 DNA levels did not significantly increase for 12 weeks post-TI but returned to pre-therapy levels by 60 weeks (p<0.0001). In 15 patients who restarted ART, reservoir size returned to pre-TI levels (p=0.58), suggesting reversibility of DNA increases.
evaluation: The dynamics of HIV-1 DNA post-TI are well-characterized (C44-C47), but the reversibility claim (C48-C49) is based on only 15 patients, which is underpowered. The interpretation that increases are "reversible" (C49) requires larger studies for confirmation. The contrast between rapid viral rebound (p<0.001 at 4 weeks) and delayed DNA increase (p=0.30) is reassuring for TI strategies.

result: Total HIV-1 DNA at TI predicted time to viral rebound to 400 copies/ml (HR=2.68, p=0.0069 in multivariable model) but not to 50 copies/ml. Integrated DNA did not predict rebound. High Total DNA was associated with first detectable viral load >400 copies/ml (p=0.0074).
evaluation: The differential prediction of rebound to 400 vs 50 copies/ml (C56-C57) is intriguing and explained by post-hoc analysis (C58) showing DNA level affects rebound magnitude. However, C58 is based on small sample (n=45) and is post-hoc, requiring validation. The failure of Integrated DNA to predict rebound (C51) contrasts with its prediction of clinical progression and warrants mechanistic investigation. The finding that baseline viral load and CD4 don't predict rebound (C54-C55) strengthens the case for HIV-1 DNA measurement.
